::: {.callout-note}
## What this page is

This is a conceptual page, so it does not add any new `plant` equations. It
uses a framework from @Dietze-2017 to separate the main sources of predictive
uncertainty, show where each one enters `plant`, and introduce ensembles as a
way to measure them. `plant` does not yet provide a complete workflow for
calibration, uncertainty propagation, or forecasting.

It helps to have read [The big picture](overview.qmd) first. The
[size-structured PDE](size-structured-pde.qmd) and [Adaptive
dynamics](adaptive-dynamics.qmd) pages give more detail on the model outputs
used as examples here.
:::

## The idea first

One run of `plant` gives one answer: a size distribution, a self-thinning
trajectory, or an invasion ratio for a chosen resident and mutant. That answer
is conditional on everything supplied to the model. Change the starting stand,
the climate drivers, or an uncertain parameter, and the answer may change too.

The useful questions are therefore: **How wide is the range of plausible
answers, and what makes it wide?** The framework below helps by naming a small
number of uncertainty sources and expressing each as a contribution to the
spread of the prediction. Once those contributions can be compared, we can
decide whether better field measurements, better environmental forecasts, or
a change to the model itself would help most.

The central lesson is simple: a model can return one repeatable answer without
that answer being certain.

## A framework for prediction

Start with a general dynamic model: one that moves a system from time $t$ to
time $t+1$. Let $Y$ be the state we want to predict:

$$Y_{t+1} = f(Y_t, X_t \mid \bar\theta + \alpha) + \varepsilon_t$$ {#eq-dietze-model}

The equation is abstract, but each symbol represents a familiar modelling
choice:

- **State variable** $Y$ is what the model carries forward through time. It
  might be biomass, population size, or an entire size distribution. The
  dependence of $Y_{t+1}$ on $Y_t$ is what makes the model dynamic.
- **Driver** (or **covariate**) $X$ is an external input, such as incoming
  light, rainfall, or a disturbance regime. The model reads a driver but does
  not calculate it as part of the state being predicted.
- **Parameter** $\theta$ is a coefficient such as a physiological rate or a
  trait value. Here it is written as $\bar\theta + \alpha$: a mean value plus
  a deviation for a particular species, site, or year. In a statistical model,
  $\alpha$ is often called a **random effect**.
- **Process error** $\varepsilon$ is variation in the real transition that the
  model does not explain. It is different from error in measuring $Y$.
- The function $f$ is the model itself: our account of how the transition
  happens.

We can now ask how uncertainty in each ingredient contributes to uncertainty
in $Y_{t+1}$. Using variance as a measure of spread gives the approximate
partition

$$\underbrace{\mathrm{Var}[Y_{t+1}]}_{\text{forecast uncertainty}} \approx
\underbrace{\left(\tfrac{\partial f}{\partial Y}\right)^{2}\!\mathrm{Var}[Y_t]}_{\text{initial conditions}} +
\underbrace{\left(\tfrac{\partial f}{\partial X}\right)^{2}\!\mathrm{Var}[X]}_{\text{drivers}} +
\underbrace{\left(\tfrac{\partial f}{\partial \theta}\right)^{2}\!\big(\mathrm{Var}[\bar\theta] + \mathrm{Var}[\alpha]\big)}_{\text{parameters + variability}} +
\underbrace{\mathrm{Var}[\varepsilon]}_{\text{process error}}$$ {#eq-partition}

This is a first-order, one-step approximation: it treats the model as locally
linear around the values being considered. The expression also assumes that
the uncertain inputs are independent. If traits vary together because of
biological trade-offs, covariance terms are needed as well. An ensemble can
retain those relationships without writing every covariance term explicitly.

Most terms have the same form: **sensitivity squared × input uncertainty**.

- **Sensitivity** is the derivative $\partial f/\partial\,\cdot$: the slope
  showing how much the prediction changes when an input changes. A highly
  influential input contributes little predictive uncertainty if its value is
  known very precisely.
- **Input uncertainty** is the corresponding $\mathrm{Var}[\,\cdot\,]$: the
  spread of plausible values for that input.
- **Process error** is different: it is added directly to the prediction rather than scaled by a local sensitivity.

The largest contributions therefore come from inputs that are both influential
and poorly known. Sensitivity alone is not enough to decide what should be
measured more carefully.

This idea also gives a practical definition of a **forecast horizon**. A
forecast remains informative while its uncertainty is smaller than a chosen
baseline, such as the natural variability of the system. The horizon is the
time, or spatial distance, at which forecast uncertainty reaches that baseline.

Initial-condition uncertainty behaves differently from the other terms because
the predicted state becomes the starting state for the next step. If the
dynamics amplify small differences
($\lvert\partial f/\partial Y\rvert > 1$), uncertainty grows from one step to
the next. If they damp those differences
($\lvert\partial f/\partial Y\rvert < 1$), uncertainty about the starting state
can fade. Parameter, driver, and process uncertainty can enter again at every
step.

::: {.callout-tip}
## A concrete way to read the equation

Suppose the target is stand biomass 50 years from now. Then $Y_t$ describes
the starting stand, $X_t$ contains environmental drivers such as rainfall and
incoming light, and $\theta$ contains traits and physiological parameters.
The function $f$ is the `plant` simulation that turns those ingredients into a
future stand. The $\varepsilon$ term represents real changes that the chosen
model and inputs still fail to explain. The rest of this page asks how much
each source would widen the range of predicted biomass.
:::

## Where `plant` sits

The partition applies to both statistical and process-based models. Dietze's
worked example is a dynamic linear model fitted to carbon-flux data. `plant`,
by contrast, builds predictions from physiological and demographic processes.
The same uncertainty categories apply, but they enter in different places:

|   | A fitted statistical model | `plant` |
|------------------------|------------------------|------------------------|
| What $f$ represents | a regression on covariates | processes such as photosynthesis, carbon allocation, hydraulics, and competition |
| Where parameters come from | estimates fitted to the target data | physiological measurements, published estimates, and model defaults; some remain uncalibrated |
| How unexplained variation enters | a residual term estimated from the data | usually no residual term in the deterministic size-structured workflow |
| What the state $Y$ can be | often one or a few measured quantities | a distribution over plant size, patch age, and strategy ([size-structured PDE](size-structured-pde.qmd)) |
| Common question | what happens next at a particular site? | how do stands develop, what equilibrium is possible, and which strategies can invade? |

Most theory pages on this site describe the deterministic size-structured
workflow: identical inputs produce identical outputs. `plant` also has a
finite-population stochastic patch simulator, but neither workflow includes a
statistical residual term fitted to field observations.

Deterministic does **not** mean free of predictive error. In this framework,
process error is the difference between a modelled transition and the real
one. It can include missing mechanisms, unrepresented variation among sites,
and ecological events absent from a particular simulation. In the
size-structured metacommunity model, random disturbance is represented through
the equilibrium distribution of patch ages implied by the chosen disturbance
regime (see [the size-structured PDE](size-structured-pde.qmd)). That captures
an average landscape effect, not the exact disturbance history of a real site.

::: {.callout-note}
## Where random assembly enters

The companion `regnans` package can build communities by drawing mutant
invaders at random. See [stochastic
assembly](adaptive-dynamics/assembly_stochastic.qmd).
:::

`plant` is designed to derive stand-level outcomes from individual growth,
mortality, and reproduction. Given its assumptions and inputs, quantities such
as stand structure, canopy light, and self-thinning emerge from those
processes rather than being prescribed directly ([The big
picture](overview.qmd)). In the language of @eq-partition, more variation is
being explained inside $f$.

Adding mechanism can reduce process error, but it also introduces parameters
and drivers that may themselves be uncertain. `plant` does not yet quantify
that trade-off in a standard workflow. Most analyses report the output from a
chosen set of inputs rather than a predictive interval.

## The five sources, in `plant`

Each term in @eq-partition has a recognisable counterpart in `plant`:

| Source | How it appears in `plant` | What it means in practice |
|------------------------|------------------------|------------------------|
| **Initial conditions** $\left(\tfrac{\partial f}{\partial Y}\right)^{2}\mathrm{Var}[Y_t]$ | The starting stand: how many seedlings, of which strategies, and at what sizes. Because many `plant` analyses target an equilibrium, we might expect some starting-state differences to decay, but that stability and its rate need to be measured for the output and parameterisation of interest. | Potentially important for near-term, site-specific runs; its long-run importance is an empirical property of the model dynamics. |
| **Drivers** $\left(\tfrac{\partial f}{\partial X}\right)^{2}\mathrm{Var}[X]$ | [Extrinsic drivers](../guides/extrinsic-drivers.qmd) include incoming light (PPFD), rainfall, vapour-pressure deficit, CO₂, and temperature. The disturbance regime is configured separately, but it is another external assumption that can be varied across forecasts. A run that supplies one fixed trajectory and disturbance regime treats them as known *within that run*; uncertainty returns when alternative plausible inputs are considered. | Likely to matter in a genuine forecast because forecasting a forest also requires forecasting its environment; whether it dominates must be measured. |
| **Parameter uncertainty** $\left(\tfrac{\partial f}{\partial \theta}\right)^{2}\mathrm{Var}[\bar\theta]$ | Trait and physiological parameters include leaf mass per area, wood density, seed mass, maximum height, and the many rates inside each strategy. They come from literature or defaults, and some are [not yet calibrated](../guides/tf24-nsc-storage.qmd). Dietze's sensitivity term asks how a chosen forecast output responds when these values shift; this is distinct from, though potentially relevant to, trait effects on invasion fitness in [Adaptive dynamics](adaptive-dynamics.qmd). | Measure parameters that are both influential and poorly known. |
| **Parameter variability / random effects** $\left(\tfrac{\partial f}{\partial \theta}\right)^{2}\mathrm{Var}[\alpha]$ | Dietze's $\alpha$ represents variation among species, sites, or years. `plant` can represent differences among strategies explicitly, but a standard strategy does not describe a distribution of traits among otherwise similar individuals. | Some variation is represented as named strategies; remaining within-strategy or among-site variation is usually omitted rather than propagated. |
| **Process error** $\mathrm{Var}[\varepsilon]$ | The engine has no explicit residual draw, but predictive process error is unknown rather than zero. It includes **structural uncertainty** — is Beer's-law light capture right? Is the [FF16](models/ff16.qmd) allocation scheme right? — as well as unrepresented heterogeneity and stochastic events. Comparing [FF16](models/ff16.qmd), [K93](models/k93.qmd), and [TF24](models/tf24.qmd) is one way to probe the structural component. | Data and model comparison reveal whether the mechanism is systematically wrong; repeated observations help estimate the remaining transition error. |

## Determinism is not certainty

Repeatability describes the calculation, not our confidence in its answer.
For a deterministic `plant` run, identical inputs give identical outputs, but
the inputs can still be uncertain:

- the parameters have error bars,
- the drivers (future climate, disturbance) are unknown,
- the initial state is only approximately known,
- and the *equations themselves* might be wrong (structural uncertainty).

The result of one run is therefore a conditional prediction: *this is the
answer if these inputs and equations are accepted*. To obtain a range, we must
propagate plausible input values through the model and account for the process
error that remains.

## Propagation and ensembles

**Uncertainty propagation** means allowing uncertain inputs to vary and
measuring the resulting spread in model outputs. Process error is then added
or estimated separately. Two broad approaches are available.

An **analytical approximation** uses the
$(\partial f/\partial\,\cdot)^2\,\mathrm{Var}$ terms in @eq-partition. It can be
computationally cheap, but it only describes local, near-linear responses.
Strong curves and thresholds in light competition or hydraulics can make that
local approximation a poor description of the full range.

An **ensemble**, also called a Monte Carlo approach, runs the full model many
times with different plausible inputs. This is a more natural candidate for a
nonlinear model such as `plant`.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Key terms

- **Monte Carlo method** — a method that answers a question using many random
  samples instead of solving the uncertainty calculation exactly.
- **Ensemble** — the collection of model runs. Each run is one **member** with
  its own sampled inputs. The distribution of outputs across members shows the
  propagated input uncertainty.
:::

### How you set one up

For `plant`, a basic ensemble would follow five steps:

1. **Describe each uncertain input with a distribution.** A trait is represented
   by plausible values rather than one fixed number. Rainfall is represented
   by plausible time series, and the starting stand by plausible initial
   states.
2. **Draw complete sets of inputs.** Each draw must contain everything needed
   for one run. Dietze's worked example uses 500 ensemble members. When runs
   are expensive, a design such as **Latin hypercube sampling** can cover each
   input distribution more evenly than simple random sampling. Correlated
   inputs must still be drawn together from a suitable joint distribution.
3. **Run the model once for each set.** Ensemble members are independent and
   can usually be distributed across processor cores.
4. **Summarise the distribution of outputs.** Report a centre, such as the
   median, alongside an interval or the full distribution. The 2.5th and 97.5th
   percentiles are often used for a central 95% interval.
5. **Compare ensembles to attribute the spread.** For example, first vary only
   the initial state, then also vary parameters, and then add uncertain drivers.
   The additional spread after each change indicates that source's contribution.
   Representing process error would require an error model fitted to
   observations. Structural uncertainty could also be explored by comparing
   several defensible model structures.

This sequential comparison is easy to understand, but the result can depend on
the order in which correlated sources are introduced. A formal variance-based
sensitivity analysis is needed when a unique allocation among interacting
sources matters.

### Two wrinkles specific to `plant`

- **Sample related traits together.** Plant traits are often correlated through
  trade-offs. Drawing leaf mass per area, wood density, and other traits
  independently can create combinations that are not biologically plausible.
  Samples should come from a joint distribution that preserves those
  relationships.
- **Do not assume the answers form a bell-shaped distribution.** Thresholds
  can produce qualitatively different outcomes. A strategy may persist in
  some ensemble members and disappear in others. In that case, the frequency
  of each outcome and the full output distribution are more informative than
  a symmetric error bar.

## Does more mechanism mean less uncertainty?

It is tempting to assume that a more detailed model must make a more precise
prediction. The uncertainty framework shows why this is not guaranteed.

Consider adding an explicit [soil-water balance](soil-water.qmd). If missing
water stress was an important source of model error, the new process may reduce
structural uncertainty. At the same time, it introduces soil and hydraulic
parameters and makes the prediction depend on rainfall. Several related
parameters are [not yet calibrated](../guides/tf24-nsc-storage.qmd), and future
rainfall is itself uncertain. Total uncertainty falls only if the better
representation of drought outweighs those new sources.

Dietze notes that common model-selection criteria balance fit against model
complexity but do not necessarily include uncertainty in future drivers. A
process can therefore improve fit while making a forecast more dependent on an
input that is difficult to predict. Soil water may be essential in a dry stand
and add little predictive value in a wet stand. The answer depends on the
system and the forecast being made.

Prediction is not the only purpose of a mechanistic model. A process can be
valuable because it lets us test a biological explanation, even if it does not
narrow a forecast interval. A model built to investigate a drought mechanism
should therefore not be judged only by short-term predictive precision.

## How field data helps

Different observations reduce different parts of @eq-partition. Matching the
data to the uncertainty source is more useful than simply collecting more of
everything.

- **Trait and demographic measurements reduce parameter uncertainty.** Under
  familiar sampling assumptions, uncertainty in a mean often falls roughly as
  $1/\sqrt{n}$ as sample size $n$ grows. Sensitivity analysis helps target this
  effort: measure parameters that are both influential and poorly known. The
  [calibration guide](../guides/calibration.qmd) is intended to develop this
  part of the workflow.
- **Independent observations reveal structural error.** Observed size
  distributions, growth, mortality, and coexistence patterns show where the
  model is systematically wrong. If errors are consistently larger in dry
  years, for example, that pattern is evidence that a water-related process or
  driver may be missing. New observations can then test whether adding that
  process actually improves predictions.
- **Stand inventories reduce uncertainty about initial conditions.** Their
  value is usually greatest for near-term, site-specific predictions. Whether
  the benefit persists depends on how quickly the model forgets its starting
  state.
- **Climate and disturbance records describe the drivers.** They reveal past
  ranges and correlations, but cannot remove uncertainty about future driver
  trajectories.
- **Repeated measurements across sites and years quantify variation.** They
  help estimate the $\alpha$ term instead of treating all among-site or
  among-year differences as unexplained scatter.

The overall workflow is iterative: make a prediction, compare it with new data,
diagnose the mismatch, update the model or its parameters, and predict again.
The aim is not merely to attach an error bar once, but to learn which part of
the prediction needs improvement.

## Status in `plant`

`plant` does not yet offer an end-to-end workflow for estimating and
propagating these uncertainty sources. Its deterministic simulations and
finite-population stochastic simulator can generate model outcomes, but they do
not by themselves estimate parameter uncertainty, structural error, or a
forecast interval from field data. The [calibration
guide](../guides/calibration.qmd) is still a stub.

This page is therefore an orientation to a future workflow, not documentation
of a finished feature. Such a workflow would estimate influential parameters,
sample plausible starting states and environmental drivers, run ensembles, and
compare their outputs with observations. That is how a single conditional
answer from `plant` could become a measured range of plausible predictions.
